name: Newton's Second Law
definition: Force equals mass times acceleration.
formula: F = ma
examples: A 5kg object with 20N force has a = 4m/s^2

name: Kinematic Equations
definition: Equations describing motion under constant acceleration.
formula: v_f = v_i + at; d = v_i*t + 0.5*a*t^2; v_f^2 = v_i^2 + 2ad
examples: v_f = 0 + 9.8*5 = 49m/s after 5 seconds of free fall

name: Projectile Motion
definition: Motion of an object projected into the air, subject only to acceleration due to gravity.
formula: y = v_iy*t - 0.5*g*t^2; x = v_ix*t; Range = v^2*sin(2θ)/g
examples: Max height: h = v_y^2 / (2g)
Ball thrown at 20m/s at 45° has range ≈ 40.8m

name: Newton's First Law
definition: An object at rest stays at rest and an object in motion stays in motion unless acted upon by a net external force.
formula: If ΣF = 0, then a = 0 (constant velocity)
examples: A hockey puck sliding on ice continues until friction stops it
Seatbelts needed because passengers continue forward during sudden stops

name: Newton's Third Law
definition: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.
formula: F_12 = -F_21 (forces are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction)
examples: Rocket propulsion: exhaust gases push down, rocket goes up
When you push a wall, the wall pushes back with equal force

name: Work-Energy Theorem
definition: The work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.
formula: W = ΔKE = KE_f - KE_i; KE = 0.5*m*v^2
examples: Work to accelerate 2kg mass from 0 to 10m/s: W = 0.5*2*10^2 = 100J
Power = Work/time = Force × velocity

name: Conservation of Momentum
definition: In a closed system, total momentum before collision equals total momentum after.
formula: Σp_before = Σp_after; p = mv
examples: 2kg at 5m/s + 3kg at 0m/s → combined 5kg at 2m/s
Impulse: J = Δp = F*Δt

name: Rotational Dynamics
definition: The study of rotating objects and angular motion.
formula: τ = I*α; L = I*ω; KE_rot = 0.5*I*ω^2
examples: Torque: τ = r × F (distance times force)
Disk: I = 0.5*m*r^2; Sphere: I = 0.4*m*r^2

name: First Law of Thermodynamics
definition: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another.
formula: ΔU = Q - W (change in internal energy = heat added - work done)
examples: Adding 100J heat and doing 60J work increases internal energy by 40J
Isobaric process: constant pressure

name: Second Law of Thermodynamics
definition: Entropy of an isolated system always increases; heat flows naturally from hot to cold.
formula: ΔS ≥ 0 for isolated system; η = 1 - T_c/T_h (Carnot efficiency)
examples: Coffee cools down, never heats up spontaneously
Perfect heat engine impossible (η < 100%)
Carnot engine between 400K and 300K: η = 25%

name: Heat Transfer
definition: Energy transfer due to temperature difference through conduction, convection, or radiation.
formula: Conduction: Q/t = kA(ΔT/d); Radiation: P = σAT^4
examples: Metal spoon conducts heat from hot soup
Convection currents in boiling water
Sun's energy reaches Earth via radiation

name: Kinetic Theory of Gases
definition: Gases consist of many particles in random motion; temperature relates to average kinetic energy.
formula: PV = nRT; KE_avg = (3/2)kT; v_rms = √(3kT/m)
examples: 1 mole gas at 273K, 1atm occupies 22.4L
Higher temperature → faster molecular motion
PV/T = constant for fixed amount of gas

name: Coulomb's Law
definition: The force between two point charges is proportional to the product of charges and inversely proportional to the square of distance.
examples: Two 1μC charges 1m apart: F = 8.99×10^-3 N
Like charges repel, opposite charges attract

name: Electric Fields and Potential
definition: Electric field is force per unit charge; electric potential is potential energy per unit charge.
formula: E = F/q = kQ/r^2; V = kQ/r; W = qΔV
examples: Uniform field between parallel plates: E = V/d
Work to move 2C charge through 10V: W = 20J
Field points from + to - charges

name: Ohm's Law and Circuits
definition: The current through a conductor is proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance.
formula: V = IR; P = IV = I^2R = V^2/R
examples: 12V across 4Ω resistor: I = 3A, P = 36W
Series: R_total = R1 + R2; Parallel: 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2

name: Magnetic Fields
definition: A magnetic field exerts force on moving charges and current-carrying wires.
formula: F = qvB*sin(θ); F = BIL*sin(θ); B from wire: B = μ_0*I/(2πr)
examples: Proton (q=1.6×10^-19C) at 1m/s in 1T field: F = 1.6×10^-19 N
Current loop creates magnetic dipole

name: Electromagnetic Induction
definition: A changing magnetic flux through a loop induces an electromotive force (EMF).
formula: ε = -dΦ_B/dt; Φ_B = B⋅A; ε = -N*dΦ/dt (Faraday's Law)
examples: Moving magnet through coil generates current
Transformers: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p
Lenz's law: induced current opposes change

name: Maxwell's Equations
definition: Four fundamental equations unifying electricity and magnetism, predicting electromagnetic waves.
examples: Electromagnetic waves travel at c = 3×10^8 m/s
Light is an electromagnetic wave
Changing E field creates B field and vice versa

name: Wave Properties
definition: Waves are disturbances that transfer energy through a medium or space.
formula: v = fλ (velocity = frequency × wavelength); T = 1/f
examples: Sound at 440Hz with λ=0.78m travels at v=343m/s
Light: f=5×10^14Hz, λ=600nm (orange)
Transverse vs longitudinal waves

name: Wave Interference and Diffraction
definition: Waves can combine (interfere) constructively or destructively; diffraction is bending around obstacles.
formula: Constructive: path difference = nλ; Destructive: path difference = (n+0.5)λ
examples: Double-slit: bright fringes at d*sin(θ) = nλ
Noise-canceling headphones use destructive interference
Water waves bend around harbor entrance

name: Doppler Effect
definition: The observed frequency of a wave changes when the source or observer is moving.
formula: f' = f(v ± v_o)/(v ∓ v_s), + for approaching, - for receding
examples: Ambulance siren sounds higher when approaching, lower when receding
Redshift of distant galaxies shows universe expansion
Radar guns use doppler shift to measure speed

name: Reflection and Refraction
definition: Light reflection obeys angle of incidence = angle of reflection; refraction is bending when entering different medium.
formula: Snell's Law: n1*sin(θ1) = n2*sin(θ2); n = c/v (refractive index)
examples: Light from air (n=1) to water (n=1.33) bends toward normal
Mirror: θ_i = θ_r
Critical angle for total internal reflection: sin(θ_c) = n2/n1

name: Lenses and Mirrors
definition: Curved surfaces that focus or diverge light through reflection or refraction.
formula: 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i; M = -d_i/d_o = h_i/h_o
examples: Convex lens: f > 0 (converging); Concave: f < 0 (diverging)
Object at 2f from lens produces real, inverted, same-size image at 2f
Magnifying glass uses convex lens

name: Wave Nature of Light
definition: Light exhibits wave properties including interference and diffraction.
formula: Young's double-slit: d*sin(θ) = mλ for bright fringes
examples: Double-slit experiment shows light interference
Thin film interference creates rainbow colors in soap bubbles
Polarized sunglasses block certain light orientations

name: Special Relativity
definition: Laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames; speed of light is constant for all observers.
formula: E = mc^2; Time dilation: Δt' = γΔt; Length contraction: L' = L/γ; γ = 1/√(1-v^2/c^2)
examples: 1kg mass has energy equivalent E = 9×10^16 J
GPS satellites account for time dilation
Nothing with mass can reach speed of light

name: Quantum Mechanics Basics
definition: Matter and energy exhibit both wave and particle properties at atomic scales.
formula: E = hf (photon energy); λ = h/p (de Broglie wavelength); ΔxΔp ≥ ℏ/2 (uncertainty)
examples: Photon with f=5×10^14Hz has E=3.3×10^-19J
Electron diffraction shows wave nature
Cannot simultaneously know exact position and momentum
Photoelectric effect proves light is quantized
